newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's crisis-ridden Bhutto down, but not out.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's crisis-ridden Bhutto down, but not out.

text.p: Pakistan's Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, facing multiple crises, will cling to power rather than step gracefully aside, analysts said on Monday.
Bhutto, 43, has sworn to ride out the political and economic storms battering her three-year-old government and seek a fresh mandate at the next elections, due to be held by October 1998.
She portrays herself abroad as a woman struggling against the odds to steer her turbulent Islamic country on a moderate course of economic liberalisation and social justice.
Her critics at home flay her for leading what they say is a corrupt, inept government that has fumbled its foreign policy, flirted with economic ruin and trampled on human rights.
"We are into our Golden Jubilee celebrations and several visits of foreign dignitaries, including the Queen (Elizabeth), are scheduled ahead," Bhutto told reporters on Sunday.
"I don't think any patriotic Pakistani would therefore wish to see the government dissolved," she declared.

A European diplomat said that evoking Pakistan's 50th anniversary, not to mention a royal visit still 12 months away, as a reason for her foes to ease up smacked of desperation. "But she is a fighter who is not going to give up easily," he said.
The diplomat said the prime minister, not reputed to be a good listener, may have become insulated from reality during three years in power, but is now belatedly aware of her danger.

"The government is paralysed, stricken," Ayaz Amir, a commentator in Dawn newspaper, told Reuters. "The agenda is being set by the president, the courts, other forces and the government is merely responding to events."
Bhutto's troubles have proliferated in the past two months.
Police in the violence-prone city of Karachi shot dead her estranged brother Murtaza and seven of his men on September 20 in circumstances now being investigated by a judicial inquiry.

Lawyers for Ghinwa Bhutto, Murtaza's widow, have accused Bhutto's husband Asif Ali Zardari, Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar and Sindh Province Chief Minister Abdullah Shah of conspiring to kill the prime minister's flamboyant brother.
The three men deny the charge. Bhutto says Murtaza's death is part of a plot against her family and has rejected the police version, which said Murtaza's bodyguards fired first.

President Farooq Leghari, empowered to sack Bhutto, rebuked her for remarks in which she hinted that his actions were part of a timetable for her removal. "We must remain responsible even in the face of adversity and personal loss," he said.
Leghari, a longtime Bhutto ally, has taken a higher profile, seeking a greater role in appointing top judges, demanding that parliament combat corruption and meeting opposition leaders.

Last month a strike called by the main opposition party led by Nawaz Sharif was followed by more dramatic anti-corruption protests by the religious Jamaat-i-Islami party that police in Islamabad and nearby Rawalpindi quelled with teargas and batons.

In the latest crisis, the Lahore High Court reinstated Manzoor Wattoo as chief minister of Punjab province on Sunday, saying that his dismissal last year, by presidential proclamation on Bhutto's recommendation, had been unlawful.

The court gave Wattoo 10 days to prove he held a majority in the Punjab provincial assembly. Bhutto's supporters have filed a no-confidence motion, believing that they can once again remove Wattoo, a wily politician who has changed sides several times.

The political dramas are unfolding against a backdrop of dire financial woes that forced the government last month to devalue the rupee and impose a tough new budgetary package to avert a possible foreign currency crisis and regain IMF favour.
Bhutto, who had held the finance portfolio herself for three years, finally gave it up this month, naming Naveed Qamar as finance minister to head a revamped economic team.
The International Monetary Fund has agreed to reactivate a stalled $600 million standby loan on tough terms, notably imposition of agricultural income tax, a provincial prerogative.
Three of the four provinces have passed the required legislation, but not Punjab, the richest and most powerful, where the assembly has previously opposed the tax.
If Bhutto hangs tough, it would take a parliamentary revolt, a presidential decision or a military coup to remove her.
The premier, who has vowed to protect defence spending from IMF-inspired cuts, may be safe from action by the army, whose generals seem to have lost their past penchant for politics.

"The military is not actively intriguing against the government," said Amir. "Certainly they are concerned about the state of the nation, but there is a tacit understanding that they want things resolved within the system."
